stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Paleobotanist Ines Carvalho reconstructs ancient forests from the fossil pollen preserved in lake sediments. Her 2021 analysis of a core drilled in northern Portugal, a column of mud recording roughly 40,000 years______ showed that oak woodland returned to the region nearly two thousand years earlier than previous studies had estimated.
explanation: The comma after "Portugal" opens a description of the core: "a column of mud recording roughly 40,000 years." A comma opened it, so a comma has to close it. Cross the phrase out and you get "Her 2021 analysis of a core drilled in northern Portugal showed that...", which is a complete sentence. The closing comma after "years" is the only thing still needed.

A.why: You put a semicolon between the subject ("Her 2021 analysis") and its verb ("showed"). A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides, and neither side is one here.

B.why: You left the interrupter open. The comma after "Portugal" started the description, and without a matching comma after "years" it never ends, so it runs straight into the main verb.

D.why: Adding "and" makes "showed" look like the second of two joined verbs. The sentence has no first verb for it to pair with, so the main clause falls apart.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Agronomists at an experimental farm in central Iowa have spent a decade testing cover crops, which are plants grown between cash-crop seasons to protect the soil. The team's best performer—cereal rye sown in late October and left standing until the following spring______ reduced the nitrate washing out of the test plots by nearly a third.
explanation: The dash after "performer" opens an interruption that names the crop and describes how it was grown. An interruption opened with a dash has to close with a dash. Remove the interruption and you get "The team's best performer reduced the nitrate...", which is a complete sentence.

B.why: You closed the interruption with a different mark from the one that opened it. A dash cannot be paired with a comma; the two ends have to match.

C.why: You left the interruption open. Without a closing dash, "spring" runs straight into "reduced," and the reader cannot tell where the extra information ends.

D.why: You put a semicolon between the subject ("The team's best performer") and its verb ("reduced"). Neither side is a complete sentence, so a semicolon cannot go here.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: When inspectors examined the Harlow Creek Bridge in 2019, they found that its original steel bearings had rusted in place, leaving the deck unable to shift. choices: expand, and contract, as temperatures change,
expand and contract as temperatures change
expand and contract as temperatures change;
expand and contract as temperatures change,
explanation: The comma after "replacements" opens a description of the pads, and that description ends at "change." Close it with a comma there and add nothing inside it. "Expand and contract" is one compound verb, and "as temperatures change" tells you when that happens, so no commas belong between them. Take the description out and "The replacements were installed..." is a complete sentence.

A.why: You scattered commas inside the description. "Expand and contract" is a single pair of verbs, and fencing off "and contract" breaks it up for no reason.

B.why: You left the description open. The comma after "replacements" needs a partner after "change"; without it, the phrase runs straight into "were installed."

C.why: You put a semicolon between the subject ("The replacements") and its verb ("were installed"). What comes before the semicolon is not a complete sentence.

stimulus: In 2016, planners in the city of Aldren closed a nine-block section of downtown to through traffic, a move that local merchants initially opposed. explanation: The comma after "feature" opens an appositive describing the plazas. It opened with a comma, so it closes with a comma after "intersections." Take it out and you get "The plan's most visible feature now draws more pedestrians...", which is grammatical.

A.why: You closed a comma-opened appositive with a dash. The marks around an interruption must match, so a comma needs a comma.

C.why: You left the appositive open. Without a closing comma, "intersections" reads as if it were the subject of "draws," and the main clause gets lost.

D.why: Adding "and" suggests two things are being joined, but "draws" is the sentence's only main verb. With "and" in front of it, the subject never gets a verb of its own.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: To test whether breakfast grains affect blood lipids, nutrition researchers assigned 140 adults to one of two diets for twelve weeks. One group, which ate oat-based porridge each morning while the other group ate refined-wheat flakes______ ended the trial with LDL cholesterol levels about 8 percent lower than the comparison group's. The researchers credit beta-glucan, a soluble fiber found in oats, for most of that gap.
explanation: The comma after "One group" opens a removable clause ("which ate oat-based porridge... refined-wheat flakes"). You close it with the same mark that opened it, a comma. Cross the clause out and the sentence still works: "One group ended the trial with LDL cholesterol levels about 8 percent lower."

B.why: A semicolon has to have a complete sentence on each side. "One group, which ate... flakes" has no main verb, so it is a fragment and cannot come before a semicolon. You needed to close the interrupter, not end the sentence.

C.why: Adding "and" pulls "ended the trial" into the which-clause, as if two actions were being joined. That leaves "One group" without a main verb. This is the trap the item is built for: you have to close the interrupter, not connect it to the next part.

D.why: The interrupter opened with a comma, so it has to close with a comma. If you open with a comma and close with a dash, the two ends don't match.

explanation: The dash after "The foreshocks" opens a long interrupter that runs to "residents." A dash pair works like a comma pair, so you close it with a second dash. A.why: The interrupter opened with a dash, so it has to close with a dash. When you close with a comma, the two ends don't match. The opening dash is far back in the sentence, which makes it easy to forget.

C.why: With no punctuation, the interrupter never closes, so "released" seems to belong inside the descriptive phrase. You lost track of where the extra information stops and the main clause starts again.

D.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence before it. "The foreshocks—a cluster of... residents" has no main verb, so it is a fragment. This choice ends a sentence where you only needed to close an interrupter.

D.why: The comma does close the interrupter, but the "and" after it turns "was eventually replaced" into a verb joined to something that has no main verb, so the subject is still left without a predicate. Close the interrupter and add nothing.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Shorebirds that migrate across open ocean cannot stop to feed or rest on the water. In 2022 a juvenile bar-tailed godwit, fitted with a five-gram satellite tag on its ______ Tasmania without once landing, covering roughly 13,500 kilometers in eleven days. choices: back by researchers in Alaska, flew to

explanation: The comma after "godwit" opens a participial phrase, "fitted with a five-gram satellite tag on its back by researchers in Alaska." That phrase is one unit and needs no commas inside it. It closes with a single comma before the main verb "flew." Cross it out and "a juvenile bar-tailed godwit flew to Tasmania" still reads correctly.

B.why: You put a comma inside the phrase, splitting "on its back" from "by researchers," and left out the comma that should close it before "flew." The comma is in the wrong place.

C.why: You never closed the interrupter. The phrase opened with a comma after "godwit," so it needs a matching comma before the main verb "flew."

D.why: You added "and" as if two actions were being joined. The phrase starting with "fitted" has no main verb of its own, so "and flew" leaves the godwit without one.
